stem: The family of a client with advanced cancer and diagnosed cachexia says, "If we can just make him eat enough calories, the muscle loss should reverse." Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: Cachexia is multifactorial and is not fully reversed by nutrition alone; nutrition support is individualized and remains one part of broader symptom and medical management.
options.B: Cachexia usually results from inadequate calorie intake, so meeting estimated calorie needs should reverse the muscle loss if the client is able to eat enough.
options.C: Because nutrition cannot reverse cachexia by itself, nutrition assessment and support provide little benefit once the wasting syndrome has been diagnosed.
options.D: A standard high-calorie meal plan is the main treatment for cachexia, while management of inflammation, symptoms, and functional problems is secondary.

rationale: The National Cancer Institute describes cancer cachexia as a multifactorial wasting syndrome with ongoing skeletal-muscle loss that cannot be fully reversed by conventional nutrition support. NCI also explains that reduced intake alone does not account for cachexia and that inflammation and metabolic changes contribute. Nutrition intervention still has a role: NCI recommends individualized nutrition therapy and identifies the registered dietitian as an integral member of the oncology team, while cachexia management may also involve medical treatment, symptom management, physical therapy, and other disciplines. Therefore A is correct. B reduces cachexia to inadequate intake, C incorrectly dismisses useful nutrition support, and D replaces individualized multidisciplinary management with a universal meal plan.
educational_objective: Differentiate cancer cachexia from simple inadequate intake: nutrition support can be useful but does not fully reverse the multifactorial wasting syndrome and should be individualized within multidisciplinary management.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Cancer Cachexia; Nutrition in Cancer Care (PDQ®) — Health Professional Version
source_locator: Cancer Cachexia > What is cancer cachexia?: cancer cachexia causes loss of skeletal muscle and fat and, unlike malnutrition, cannot be reversed with nutrition support alone. > What causes cancer cachexia?: inflammation, increased metabolism, insulin resistance, and hormone changes may contribute. > Ways to manage cancer cachexia: multidisciplinary care may include medical treatment, a registered dietitian, nutrition support, and physical therapy. Nutrition in Cancer Care (PDQ) > Tumor metabolism/Anorexia and Cachexia: energy deficit alone does not explain cachexia and increased caloric intake has failed to counteract the wasting process. > Methods of Nutrition Therapy: use an individualized approach to oral, enteral, and parenteral nutrition. > Counseling by a registered dietitian: the registered dietitian/nutritionist is an integral member of the oncology team.
source_claim_supported: Cancer cachexia is a multifactorial wasting syndrome not fully reversed by nutrition alone; nutrition assessment and individualized support remain appropriate as part of multidisciplinary management.

supporting_sources.organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
supporting_sources.document_title: Nutrition in Cancer Care (PDQ®) — Health Professional Version
supporting_sources.locator: Tumor metabolism/Anorexia and Cachexia: cachexia is multifactorial and cannot be fully reversed by conventional nutrition support; energy deficit alone does not explain the syndrome. Methods of Nutrition Therapy: individualized nutrition intervention is used for precachexia/cachexia. Counseling by a registered dietitian: the dietitian is an integral oncology-team member.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Nutrition remains individualized and clinically relevant in cachexia even though increased intake alone does not reverse the wasting syndrome.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort > Nutrition and Oral Hydration, printed pp. 36–37 (PDF pp. 39–40): evaluate the client's nutritional status and intervene as needed; provide and maintain special diets based on diagnosis/nutritional needs; provide nutritional supplements as needed; evaluate the impact of disease/illness on the nutritional status of a client.
blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — individualized nutrition support in cancer cachexia
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four responses to remove the absolute-word cue and uniquely-long keyed answer. The corrected distractors represent realistic misconceptions about cachexia as simple starvation, the mistaken conclusion that nutrition has no role, and a universal high-calorie plan. The keyed response is limited to directly supported claims about multifactorial pathophysiology and individualized multidisciplinary care.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Advanced cancer — cachexia and individualized nutrition management
audit_findings.stem: PASS — clearly distinguishes diagnosed cachexia from generic weight loss and asks for correction of one common family misconception.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly reflects NCI's multifactorial definition, the limitation of nutrition alone, and the continuing role of individualized nutrition within broader management; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — increased intake can support nutrition but inadequate calories alone do not explain cachexia and sufficient intake does not reliably reverse the wasting process.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — the premise that nutrition alone is insufficient is true, but NCI explicitly retains individualized nutrition assessment/support and dietitian involvement.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — high-calorie strategies may be useful for selected clients, but NCI does not support one standard meal plan as the main universal treatment or relegation of other contributors to a secondary role.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only response that accurately states both the limitation and the appropriate continuing role of nutrition support.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B equates cachexia with inadequate intake, C wrongly abandons nutrition support, and D universalizes a meal plan and minimizes broader management.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — options are comparable in length and complexity and no keyed-only absolute wording remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Basic Care and Comfort explicitly includes evaluation of nutritional status, diagnosis-based nutrition interventions, supplements, and the impact of illness on nutrition.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether C could be defended because NCI says nutrition alone cannot reverse cachexia; NCI simultaneously recommends individualized nutrition intervention and dietitian involvement, so C overreaches and A remains uniquely correct.
